Summary (auto): Technical deep dive on autoscaling and capacity planning for Redwood Dedicated/Private deployments. Focus on burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPUs, and interactions with KV cache, batching, and quantization. Action items and next steps captured at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, I have Ethan with me, our solutions engineer, and we'll run through autoscaling and capacity planning for your private deployment.
[00:18] Sofia (Nimbus): Hey Maya, thanks. Quick ask — we're trying to get predictable p95 latency under 300ms for user-facing endpoints and also want to not overprovision GPUs. So, how do you approach burst capacity?
[00:32] Ethan (Redwood SE): Yeah, great question. So broadly we use a combination of reserved capacity for steady-state and a controlled burst policy for spikes. Reserved GPUs cover your baseline QPS, and then we have transient pools that can autoscale up. There's a queueing layer with configurable admission control to protect latency SLOs.
[00:50] Liam (Nimbus CTO): When you say "transient pools", is that pre-warmed or cold? Warm starts matter a lot for us.
[00:58] Ethan: We try to keep a small warm buffer; by default we recommend keeping 10-20% of burst capacity pre-warmed depending on traffic variability. Cold starts happen if you exceed both reserved + warm buffers; then we do a gradual spin-up and fall back to slightly lower model variants to preserve latency.
[01:18] Marcus (DevOps): Can you explain the fallback logic? Lower model variants — do you mean quantized or smaller architecture?
[01:26] Ethan: Exactly, two levers: model variant (e.g., 13B -> 7B) and quantization profiles. If strict latency is required we can route to a quantized variant or trimmed model with lower token throughput but faster per-token latency. There is also admission control such that long requests can be queued or rate-limited depending on policy.
[01:50] Priya (ML Eng): How does KV cache behave across autoscaled instances? If I have many short chat sessions, KV cache hits are critical for cost and latency.
[01:59] Ethan: KV cache is sticky to the serving instance; for Dedicated we recommend session affinity for chat to keep KV locality. For burst pools we maintain a lightweight shared prefix cache—it's not as fast as local KV but helps with common prefixes. There's also a distributed cache mode for Private deployments if you want stronger sharing, though it's an additional operational tradeoff.
[02:22] Sofia: Is there instrumentation we can get to see cache hit rates across pools?
[02:26] Maya: Yes, in the Redwood Console we surface token-level cache hit/miss, per-route latency, and per-pool utilization. We'll include some sample dashboards in the runbook.
[02:40] [timestamp glitch] Speaker 1: uh-huh, yeah so the th- the slot allocation is dynamic.
[02:48] Ethan: (laughs) apologies for the ASR. Back to queueing — we model requests as M/M/c for rough sizing, but we prefer empirical histograms from customer traffic. That lets us recommend reserved capacity to hit target p95 given a per-GPU throughput curve which is a function of model, sequence length, batching config, and quantization.
[03:12] Priya: We have a bimodal traffic pattern — lots of short chat messages and occasional long form generation for batch jobs. Does Redwood separate those?
[03:20] Ethan: Yes we recommend multi-queue routing: a low-latency queue for short interactive requests with strict SLOs and a background queue for long generative jobs. Background jobs can be batched aggressively and routed to cheaper instances or lower quality tiers. This is both a cost and latency lever.
[03:38] Liam: What about batching — automatic versus explicit? We run into issues where automatic batching increases latency for interactive traffic.
[03:46] Ethan: We have workload-aware batching. For interactive routes we set small max batch sizes and aggressive max-latency thresholds so you get minimal added latency. For background routes, we allow larger batch windows. You can also pin routes to dedicated pools with different batchers.
[04:00] Sofia: Quantization — you mentioned profiles. How deterministic are the perf gains? We've seen 4-bit quant sometimes produce odd quality regressions.
[04:10] Ethan: Right, quantization gains depend on model architecture and evals. We recommend a staged approach: run evals on your prompt set across quantization profiles and measure quality/regression alerts. Our Optimize tooling will suggest quant profiles that historically give >2-3x throughput with acceptable quality on similar workloads. We'll share examples in the cost spreadsheet.
[04:32] Marcus: For Private/VPC, any networking constraints for autoscaling? We have strict peering rules and long corp firewall windows.
[04:40] Maya: For Private we offer a control plane with customer-managed networking and support VPC peering and private link. Autoscaling still needs to provision worker instances in your subnet; so subnets/CIDR and IP quotas matter. We'll coordinate with your infra to pre-approve ranges.
[04:56] Marcus: That was my next question — do you need permissions to call our cloud API to spin up GPUs?
[05:02] Ethan: For on-prem or air-gapped, we provide an operator (helm charts) and you manage the nodes; for cloud Private deployments we ask for IAM roles with scoped permissions; we can also do a managed-provider mode where Redwood operates the infra under an SLA.
[05:18] Priya: Regarding prediction of load — do you support scheduled scaling for known windows?
[05:24] Ethan: Yes, you can set scheduled policies and also burst policies based on short-term autoscaling (reactive) and scheduled (proactive). We also allow a predictive autoscaler that uses recent traffic histograms to pre-warm capacity.
[05:40] Liam: Cost question — how do reserved GPUs pricing compare to on-demand in your model?
[05:46] Maya: We'll send the cost model spreadsheet, but typical delta is 20-50% savings for reserved capacity depending on commit term and region. The spreadsheet has examples showing cost per effective token accounting for cache hits and batching.
[06:02] Sofia: Can you walk through an example: we expect 500 RPS steady with 3-second average generation and p95 target 300ms. How do you size?
[06:12] Ethan: Quick back-of-envelope — a 3s avg generation is long; for interactive p95 300ms you'd need a separate low-latency route for short completions. For the 500 RPS long jobs, we'd route to background queue and size reserved GPUs based on throughput curves. We'd need your token lengths distribution; can you share histograms?
[06:30] Priya: I can pull that after the call.
[06:34] Ethan: Perfect. For the low-latency path, if requests are <50 tokens, you can serve many QPS per GPU with small batching and KV cache; that helps keep p95 low.
[06:46] [crosstalk] Liam: So the two-queue approach seems key.
[06:50] Ethan: Exactly — separate control planes for latency-sensitive vs throughput workloads.
[06:56] Sofia: About throttling — if we hit network issues or congestion, will Redwood start failing requests? We need graceful degradation strategies.
[07:04] Ethan: We have a layered fallback: first admission control and backpressure; then model fallback; last resort is HTTP 429 or soft degrade with partial responses depending on route configs. You can set per-route fallback policies.
[07:18] Marcus: Any concerns about stateful sessions when failing over to different model variants or instances?
[07:24] Ethan: State (KV cache) is the tricky part. With session affinity we preserve local KV; when failing over we can transfer minimal prefix state or instruct clients to rehydrate context. We'll include recommended session-affinity TTLs.
[07:40] Maya: Quick note on monitoring — you should instrument client-side latency histograms as well. The Console pulls server-side metrics but client-side capture helps diagnose network versus server time.
[07:52] Priya: Security question — reserved instances in Private, who has access to logs and model cache?
[07:58] Maya: For Private deployments, logs and KV are in your VPC; we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key management. Audit logs and RBAC are configurable; we'll attach SOC2 and compliance docs.
[08:12] Sofia: Great. Can we see a sample runbook for autoscaling policies?
[08:16] Maya: Yes, we'll send a runbook with recommended thresholds, sample HPA-like policies, and burst policy examples.
[08:24] [00:08:25] Ethan: One more operational tip — set a conservative pre-warm for predictable spike windows and configure a max-burst-percent so costs don't blow out. For example, 50% max burst above reserved gives cushion without unlimited spend.
[08:40] Liam: On benchmarking, can Redwood run a synthetic load against our staging VPC?
[08:45] Ethan: Yes, we can run benchmarks with a signed-off test harness. We'll need credentials and a staging endpoint; we'll scope the test to not hit prod.
[08:56] Priya: We also want quantization experiments — could you run those with our prompt set?
[09:00] Ethan: Absolutely. We'll run evals across quantization profiles and report quality deltas along with throughput/latency.
[09:08] [minor ASR error] Speaker 2: the the run hook will be doc'd, yeah.
[09:15] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps.
[09:18] Maya: Action items: Maya will send security docs and the autoscaling runbook; Ethan will prepare the benchmark plan and test harness; Priya will share the traffic histograms and target prompt set. We'll also schedule the in-prod benchmark once infra is ready.
[09:36] Sofia: That works. Any open questions on our side?
[09:40] Liam: None immediate. We'll need to confirm subnet quotas with networking team.
[09:44] Marcus: I'll handle that and loop Marcus, sorry, I'll loop in networking.
[09:48] Maya: Great — we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the benchmark kickoff.
[09:54] Priya: Thanks all.
[09:56] Maya: Thanks, everyone, we'll send notes.
